pr_title: core: Loosen output value sensitivity requirement
pr_body:
Non-root module outputs no longer strip sensitivity marks from their values, allowing dynamically sensitive values to propagate through the configuration. We also remove the requirement for non-root module outputs to be defined as sensitive if the value is marked as sensitive.

This avoids a static/dynamic clash when using shared modules that might unknowingly receive sensitive values via input variables.

Fixes #28431.

issue_context.title: v0.15 - Passing a sensitive value to a non-sensitive module variable causes an error if the module derives a non-sensitive output from that variable
issue_context.body:
<!--
Hi there,

Thank you for opening an issue. Please note that we try to keep the Terraform issue tracker reserved for bug reports and feature requests. For general usage questions, please see: https://www.terraform.io/community.html.

If your issue relates to a specific Terraform provider, please open it in the provider's own repository. The index of providers is at https://github.com/terraform-providers.

To fix problems, we need clear reproduction cases - we need to be able to see it happen locally. A reproduction case is ideally something a Terraform Core engineer can git-clone or copy-paste and run immediately, without inventing any details or context. 

* A short example can be directly copy-pasteable; longer examples should be in separate git repositories, especially if multiple files are needed
* Please include all needed context. For example, if you figured out that an expression can cause a crash, put the expression in a variable definition or a resource
* Set defaults on (or omit) any variables. The person reproducing it should not need to invent variable settings
* If multiple steps are required, such as running terraform twice, consider scripting it in a simple shell script. For example, see [this case](https://github.com/danieldreier/terraform-issue-reproductions/tree/master/25719). Providing a script can be easier than explaining what changes to make to the config between runs.
* Omit any unneeded complexity: remove variables, conditional statements, functions, modules, providers, and resources that are not needed to trigger the bug
* When possible, use the [null resource](https://www.terraform.io/docs/providers/null/resource.html) provider rather than a real provider in order to minimize external dependencies. We know this isn't always feasible. The Terraform Core team doesn't have deep domain knowledge in every provider, or access to every cloud platform for reproduction cases.

-->

### Terraform Version
<!---
Run `terraform version` to show the version, and paste the result between the ``` marks below.

If you are not running the latest version of Terraform, please try upgrading because your issue may have already been fixed.
-->

```
0.15.0
```

### Terraform Configuration Files
<!--
Paste the relevant parts of your Terraform configuration between the ``` marks below.

For Terraform configs larger than a few resources, or that involve multiple files, please make a GitHub repository that we can clone, rather than copy-pasting multiple files in here. For security, you can also encrypt the files using our GPG public key at https://www.hashicorp.com/security.
-->

```terraform
variable "db_username" {
  description = "Database administrator username"
  type        = string
  sensitive   = true
}

module "rds" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/rds/aws"
  version = "2.34.0"

  username = var.db_username

  # additional arguments ...
}
```

### Expected Behavior
<!--
What should have happened?
-->
Both `plan` and `apply` commands should proceed successfully, redacting the passed in `username` argument (and any derived uses) from CLI output as `(sensitive value)`.

### Actual Behavior
<!--
What actually happened?
-->
Terraform errors out on plan creation with the message:
```
│ Error: Output refers to sensitive values
│
│   on .terraform/modules/rds/modules/db_instance/outputs.tf line 76:
│   76: output "this_db_instance_username" {
│
│ Expressions used in outputs can only refer to sensitive values if the sensitive attribute is true.
```
* Note that the error is coming from an output within the module (actually coming from a submodule output that is getting threaded through).
* The issue occurs regardless of whether the output is used or completely ignored.
* This did not cause an error in Terraform 0.14.x, however Terraform 0.14 ended up not treating the value as sensitive within the module (equivalent to if `username = nonsensitive(var.db_username)` had been passed into the module).
### Steps to Reproduce
<!--
Please list the full steps required to reproduce the issue, for example:
1. `terraform init`
2. `terraform apply`
-->
1. `terraform init`
2. `terraform plan` or `terraform apply`
### Additional Context
<!--
Are there anything atypical about your situation that we should know? For example: is Terraform running in a wrapper script or in a CI system? Are you passing any unusual command line options or environment variables to opt-in to non-default behavior?
-->

The author of the module did not mark the `username` input variable or the `this_db_instance_username` output as `sensitive = true`, since not all users of the module may consider the administrative username as sensitive for their particular use case or security posture (unlike an argument like `password`, which can be presumed as sensitive in all use cases). However, because the module output `this_db_instance_username` is derived from the input variable `username`, it causes an error when the value passed into `username` is being tracked as sensitive by Terraform.

The requirement for module outputs to be marked with `sensitive = true` should be limited to values and variables defined within the module as sensitive, not values that were marked as sensitive outside the module and then passed into the module through input variables not marked as sensitive. It is impractical for Terraform to force the author of third-party modules to determine what inputs/outputs all users of the module may consider sensitive, as this may vary by use case. Instead, it should allow allow sensitive values passed into a module (and any derived values) to be outputted, without the module author being concerned about whether the passed in value was marked as sensitive by the user. At the very least, the error message is misleading as it implies an issue in the module, when really it was caused by the user passing a sensitive value into the module which the module did not consider sensitive, deriving an output from that value that it did not explicitly mark as sensitive.

### References
<!--
Are there any other GitHub issues (open or closed) or Pull Requests that should be linked here? For example:

- #6017

-->
comments:
Hi @chrizkim!

I just wanted to say a little here because I noticed that PR #28472 closed this automatically but we didn't actually talk here about the problem first.

This situation arose because of a safety rule added in Terraform v0.14 where we required setting `sensitive = true` on an output value as a declaration of intent to include a sensitive value in it, because root module output values are consumable via some additional channels than other data in the Terraform configuration and so are worthy of some additional thought and scrutiny.

However, that rationale only really applies strongly to outputs declared in the _root_ module, because descendent module output values only exist transiently in memory during a Terraform operation and so don't get exported in that same way.

As a compromise then, #28472 has adjusted the rule to apply only to output values in a root module, and thus a shared module is no longer required to statically declare an output value as sensitive in order that a dynamically-inferred sensitive value might pass through it. This should therefore resolve the problem that a shared module can't practically anticipate what might be sensitive in arbitrary data provided by a calling module.

The rule still applies to root module input variables for the reason I mentioned above, but we expect that to be okay in practice because the author of the root module is ultimately in control of where all of the output value data is coming from. We also updated the error message to include some more details about why this rule exists and what to do about it.

This fix will be included in the forthcoming v0.15.1 release, which is due soon once we land a few other important fixes that are still in progress.

Thanks for reporting this!

@apparentlymart Thanks, really appreciate you taking the time to provide an update! I totally agree that the constraint is valid for root module outputs, as the author/runner has full control of configuration input/output values. One question that remains for me, will CLI output of attributes for resource created in the submodule still treat the value as sensitive? For the example in the original description, using 0.14.7 I remember seeing that the `module.rds.aws_db_instance.username` showed up un-redacted in the CLI output, even though the `username` value passed into the module had been marked as sensitive. NBD if unsure, was just curious but I can test it out in 0.15.1.

@alisdair Thanks for jumping on a fix so quickly here!

review_comments: Not really a big deal, but I think a simpler (and less expensive) way to achieve `hasSensitive` here might be `val.HasMark("sensitive")`, since it seems like we're just discarding the unmarked value above anyway.
Ahh yes, right... there isn't a `HasMarkDeep` (or such) method, so we're using `UnmarkDeep` here to get the effect of one. Seems reasonable!
